lesson.title: Putting It All Together: Building the Confidence Interval
lesson.summary: A confidence interval combines a point estimate and a margin of error into a full range of plausible values for a population parameter, expressed as estimate plus or minus margin of error.
lesson.body:
Every piece is now in place. A confidence interval is built with one simple formula: point estimate, plus or minus, margin of error. That is it. The point estimate, like p-hat or x-bar, locates the center of the interval, and the margin of error, critical value times standard error, determines how far the interval extends in each direction. Everything from the last several chapters, statistics, sampling distributions, standard error, and critical values, exists to make this one calculation trustworthy.

The formula works because of exactly the machinery built up earlier in this unit. The CLT and its conditions guarantee the sampling distribution of the statistic is approximately normal. The standard error measures its typical spread. The critical value, tied to a chosen confidence level, stretches that spread out to cover a specific target percentage of possible sample outcomes. Add all three together correctly, and the result is an interval with a mathematically justified relationship to the true parameter, not just an arbitrary range someone picked.

Return to the transit survey one final time: p-hat equals 0.25, n equals 400, standard error approximately 0.0217. For a 95% confidence interval, the margin of error, computed in the last chapter, is approximately 0.0425. The confidence interval is therefore 0.25 minus 0.0425 to 0.25 plus 0.0425, which is 0.2075 to 0.2925. In percentage terms, a statistician would report: "We are 95% confident that the true proportion of adults in the city who support the transit measure is between 20.75% and 29.25%." The precise meaning of that "95% confident" phrase, and a common misinterpretation to avoid, is the subject of a dedicated chapter shortly.

For the bottling example, x-bar equals 500 milliliters, and the 95% margin of error was approximately 2.77 milliliters. The confidence interval is 500 minus 2.77 to 500 plus 2.77, which is 497.23 to 502.77 milliliters. This tells a plant manager a full plausible range for the true average fill volume of the entire production process, not just a single number that offers no sense of how precise it is.
